  "text": "My father brought his ladder on Sunday, though I had told him the gutter could wait.

“Rain won't,” he said.

He stood in the garden looking up. One foot of the ladder sank into the flower bed.

“Hold that.”

“I could go up.”

“You could hold it.”

I pressed my shoes against the bottom rung. He climbed slowly, stopping halfway to move a clothes peg from his pocket to his mouth.

“What’s that for?”

He took it out again.

“Found it in the car.”

At the top, he reached into the gutter and dropped a handful of black leaves into the bucket I held below him. Some missed.

“Sorry.”

“You aimed.”

“Bit out of practice.”

When I was little, he had cleaned our gutters every autumn. My job was to keep my mother talking in the kitchen so she wouldn't come outside and tell him to get down.

“There's a ball up here,” he said.

“Previous owners, probably.”

He held it out: yellow, split along the seam.

“Still want it?”

“No.”

He put it in his pocket anyway.

Coming down, he felt for each rung with his heel. I kept both hands on the ladder until he stood beside me.

“I'll make tea,” I said.

“Better wash first.”

At the sink, he couldn't get the soap dispenser to work. I turned the nozzle and pressed it into his palm.

“Newfangled,” he said.

“You've got the same one.”

“Your mother fills it.”

He dried his hands, then wiped the muddy marks he'd left on the tap."
